skills.name: build

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development

skills.name: gdb-debugging

skills.name: kernel-development

skills.name: library-development

skills.name: troubleshooting

skills.name: user-app-development

# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_physical_memory_regions` — iterates a std
  `alloc::collections::LinkedList` via `for region in list.iter()`. The build
  toolchain's `vstd` (`/mnt/toolchain/verus/vstd`) ships ghost-iterator specs only
  for `slice`/`vec`/`VecDeque`/`BTree*`/`Hash*` iterators, **not** `LinkedList`, and
  the orphan rule forbids supplying `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` impls for the
  foreign `linked_list::Iter` from the `kernel` crate (E0117). Genuine Verus
  front-end limitation, not a proof gap or code bug — full analysis in
  `verus-unsupported.md`. The abstract booking effect is specified over
  `PhysMemView` and discharged (no `admit`) by
  `lemma_book_region_reserves_region_frames` in `mod.proof.rs`. `ensures` keeps the
  caller-relevant guarantee: allocator stays initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same std-`LinkedList`
  iteration limitation as above. Abstract effect (skip-if-not-covered; book tracked
  frames) discharged by `lemma_book_mmio_skip_untracked` /
  `lemma_book_mmio_books_tracked`. `ensures` keeps allocator initialized and
  well-formed across booking.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## Skip / exclude from current proof target

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## Allowed `external_body` — frame allocator core (`frame.rs`)

`frame.rs` is now the proof target. Two layers form the trust boundary of the
global frame-allocator singleton; everything else in the module (the `frame::*`
free-function shims) is **body-verified** against these contracts.

### 1. The singleton bridge: `instance()`

`instance()` returns `&'static mut Inner` obtained from the module-level
`static mut INSTANCE` via `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`. The verifier
does not support `static mut` paths, and a zero-argument uninterpreted
`phys_view()` cannot be tied to that static by any verifiable means. `instance()`
is therefore the bridge axiom: `requires phys_view().initialized` (the real panic
gate) and `ensures (*result).inv() && (*result)@ == phys_view().frames`. This is
what lets the query shims (`is_covered`, `refcount`) be fully body-verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — `static mut` singleton accessor;
  bridges the live `Inner` to the abstract `phys_view().frames`.

### 2. The `Inner::*` methods

Each `Inner::*` method has a rich, do-not-modify `old(self)@ → final(self)@`
transition contract, but its **body** cannot be translated by Verus: every method
uses the `error!` / `debug_assert_eq!` macros (whose expansion needs
`core::fmt::Arguments`, unsupported — the same limitation already recorded for
`UserFrame::drop`) and the `arch` newtypes `FrameNumber` / `FrameAddress`
(external types with no `external_type_specification`). They are `external_body`
with their pre-existing `#[verus_spec]` contracts honored as trust boundaries.

- `Inner::alloc`, `Inner::alloc_contiguous`, `Inner::free`, `Inner::share`,
  `Inner::refcount`, `Inner::book`, `Inner::is_covered`, `Inner::alloc_range`
  (all in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs`).

### Note on the body-verified shims

The `frame::*` free-function shims are no longer `external_body`. The pure-query
shims `is_covered` and `refcount` are proven outright via the `instance()` bridge.
The aggregate query shim `free_count` is also fully body-verified via
`lemma_free_count` (`frame.proof.rs`): it counts the clear bitmap indices as the
image of an injective `i -> i * page_size` map and discharges
`free_frames.len() + usage == num_bits` without any `admit()`.

The mutating reservation shims (`alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`, `book`,
`alloc_range`, `share`) are body-verified and carry the **strong** post-state
contract via the `tracked PhysAuth` carrier threaded through `&mut`: each names
both `old(auth)@` (pre-state) and `final(auth)@` (post-state) and asserts the
exact `FrameAllocView` transition (`spec_alloc_one` / `spec_alloc_set` /
`spec_share`), with a meaningful `Err` arm (`final(auth)@ == old(auth)@`). They
carry no `admit()`.

## Allowed `external_body` — `frame::free` (`frame.rs`, `Drop` path)

`frame::free` is reached only from `UserFrame::drop` / `KernelFrame::drop`. Their
trait-fixed `drop(&mut self)` signature is `opens_invariants none` + `no_unwind`,
so the `Drop` path **cannot** receive a `Tracked<&mut PhysAuth>` carrier and
**cannot** open a global invariant to reach the authority. Without the token the
body cannot discharge `instance()`'s `phys_view().initialized` precondition nor
`Inner::free`'s `frame.inv()` precondition, and the contract must stay
precondition-free for `Drop` soundness. The function is therefore `external_body`
with its weak, always-true `ensures phys_view().inv()` honored as a trust boundary
(the logging branch performs no state change). This replaces the previous deferred
`proof! { admit(); }`; the trust surface is identical, but `external_body` is the
governed mechanism. It is the single deliberate, caller-justified `Drop`-path
exception — **not** the forbidden weakening, which concerned the reservation ops
that now carry the strong `PhysAuth`-threaded post-state.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference on `Drop`.
  `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path; no precondition (`Drop`-safe).

## Allowed `external_body` — `UserFrame::drop` (`upool.rs`)

`UserFrame::drop` releases the frame's reference by calling `frame::free` and, on
the error path, logs via the `error!` macro. The `error!`/`write!` expansion uses
`core::fmt` Debug formatting (`{:?}`), which Verus cannot translate to VIR
("Unsupported constant type"). The function is therefore `external_body`; its
`#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by trusting that body. The contract is not a
new guarantee — `ensures phys_view().inv()` is exactly the post-state already
established by the `external_body` `frame::free` shim it calls, and the logging
branch performs no state change. `opens_invariants none` / `no_unwind` record that
`drop` opens no invariant and cannot unwind (errors are logged, not propagated).

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::<UserFrame as Drop>::drop` — releases one
  reference on scope exit. `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path.

## Allowed `external_body` — `PhysMemoryManager` (`manager.rs`)

`PhysMemoryManager` is a **stateless facade** over the global frame allocator
(`Upool` has no fields; kernel frames are drawn from the global `frame::*`
statics through `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER`). Its target methods therefore
have no verifiable body: they mutate global `static mut` state, call un-specced
upstream allocator primitives, and use side-effecting combinators
(`inspect_err`/`and_then`/`ok_or_else`) and `error!`/`warn!` macros that are not
ghost-gated and have no `vstd` specs. They form a trust boundary identical in
character to the `frame.rs` shims: each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over the do-not-modify `phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView` and the
returned frame values (monotone post-state facts, as there is no
`old(phys_view())`). Abstract laws are carried by `manager.proof.rs` lemmas.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::init` — writes the
  global `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER` (`MaybeUninit::write`) and flips an
  `AtomicBool`. `ensures` keeps the allocator initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` —
  draws a frame from the global allocator and wraps it as a `UserFrame`.
  `ensures` (on success) places the returned frame's address in
  `allocated_frames` and states page alignment.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::check_user_watermark` —
  reads the build-time `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK` and the global free
  count. `ensures` (on success) gives `spec_watermark_ok` and keeps
  `free_frames` finite.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_user_frames`
  — loop-allocates `count` user frames into a caller `&mut Vec`, with all-or-
  nothing cleanup. `ensures` gives `len == count` and each frame allocated on
  success, empty vector on error.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_kernel_frame` —
  like `alloc_user_frame` but yields a `KernelFrame`.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_kernel_frames`
  — like `alloc_many_user_frames` plus the contiguity guarantee
  (`kernel_frames_contiguous`) required for kernel stacks.

## Allowed `external_body` — not-yet-verified dependencies of `mm::phys::kframe`

`KernelFrame::new` is the first verified (`#[verus_spec]`) exec body in the proof
target that calls cross-module address-conversion / mapping helpers. Those helpers
live in `hal::mem` and `mm::virt`, which are **not yet verified**, so they are
declared outside any `verus!` macro and Verus would otherwise reject the call.
Each is given a temporary `external_body` `#[verus_spec]` contract so the verified
`new` body type-checks; the contracts are removed when their home modules are
verified. None weakens an existing guarantee — they only name facts `new` already
relies on (newtype address identity) or state nothing observable (the
identity-map side effect, which no `mm::phys` contract names).

41. pub struct ExFrameNumber(FrameNumber);

43. // ── Frame-number trust-boundary projections (arch `FrameNumber`) ──────────────
44. //
45. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
46. // `View` impl reachable here (orphan rule). Its abstract index is therefore
47. // projected by an uninterpreted ghost function, exactly as `view_design.md`
48. // prescribes. `spec_max_frame_number()` denotes `FrameNumber::MAX`.
49. 
50. // The integer index of a frame number (`0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`).
51. pub uninterp spec fn spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int;
52. 
53. // The largest representable frame number. Mirrors `arch FrameNumber::MAX ==
54. // MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1 == usize::MAX / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. Interpreting it
55. // against `usize::MAX` and `spec_page_size()` is what lets verified constructors
56. // discharge their `usize` multiply (no-overflow) obligation: a frame index in
57. // `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()` scaled by `spec_page_size()` stays `<= usize::MAX`.
58. pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
59.     usize::MAX as int / spec_page_size() - 1
60. }
61. 
62. // ── Derived spec helpers over the View domain (`int`) ─────────────────────────
63. 
64. // The frame an address lies in: exact integer division, independent of whether
65. // the implementation shifts (`>> FRAME_SHIFT`) or divides (`/ FRAME_SIZE`).
66. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
67.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
68. }
69. 
70. // The base (frame-aligned) address of a frame index: `frame * FRAME_SIZE`.
71. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
72.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
73. }
74. 
75. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
76. 
77. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
78. // canonical `spec_page_size()`. It is strictly positive (`== 4096`); positivity is
79. // the load-bearing fact for the division/modulo reasoning in the constructors.
80. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
81.     ensures
82.         result == spec_page_size(),
83.         spec_page_size() > 0,
84. ;
85. 
86. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
87. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined, and `2^FRAME_SHIFT == FRAME_SIZE`
88. // so the shift coincides with division by `spec_page_size()`.
89. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
90.     ensures
91.         result < usize::BITS,
92.         pow2(result as nat) == spec_page_size(),
93. ;
94. 
95. // `VirtualAddress::new` is a pure newtype constructor: the wrapped value is the
96. // abstract address. (`sys` library edge; the inner module is not yet verified.)
97. pub assume_specification[ VirtualAddress::new ](value: usize) -> (result: VirtualAddress)
98.     ensures
99.         result@ == value as int,
100. ;
101. 
102. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
103. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address.
104. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
105.     addr: VirtualAddress,
106. ) -> (result: usize)
107.     ensures
108.         result as int == addr@,
109. ;
110. 
111. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
112. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
113. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
114.     ensures
115.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
116.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
117. ;
118. 
119. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
120. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
121.     ensures
122.         match result {
123.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
124.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
125.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
126.         },
127. ;
128. 
129. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
130. //
131. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
132. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
133. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
134. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
135. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
136. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
137. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).
138. impl PhysicalAddress {
139.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
140.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
141.     }
142. }
143. 
144. } // verus!
145.

---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers verus! block syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**Iterator rewrite rule:** When exec code uses Iterator chains
(`.iter().filter().map().collect()`), these MUST be rewritten to while
loops because Iterator API is unsupported. This is a permitted exec
change because: (1) the behavioral semantics are identical, (2) it is
a true Verus limitation, (3) the ensures should describe the ORIGINAL
functional intent using `Seq::filter`/`Seq::map_values`, not the
rewritten loop structure.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Banned **as a workaround** for spec/proof difficulty. Permitted ONLY for functions that use a True Limitation feature (async, float arithmetic, transmute, static mut) — see True Limitations table below. ## Spec Vocabulary Reference

When writing spec, you have these tools. Each includes **when to use** (not just what it is):

**choose:** `choose|x: T| P(x)` — Use when you have `exists|x| P(x)` and need a concrete witness value in a spec expression. Without this, you cannot define spec functions that "pick" a satisfying element.

**Extensional equality:** `=~=` for Seq/Set/Map, `=~~=` for nested collections. In many simple cases `==` also works for Seq, but when Z3 struggles with collection equality, switch to `=~=`. **Guideline: start with `==`, use `=~=` if Z3 can't prove it.**

**old():** `old(self)@` in ensures of `&mut` functions. **Test: does this function take &mut? Then ensures MUST contain old().** Without this, ensures compares new state to itself (tautological).

**ghost struct:** Use when you need a spec-only abstraction that has no exec counterpart. Example: an `Interval { lo: int, hi: int }` for reasoning about address ranges that don't exist as a runtime type.

**spec_fn:** `spec_fn(T) -> U` — Use when a spec needs to be parameterized by a function. Example: a generic "map" spec that takes a transformation function.

**Seq operations in spec:** Even though `Iterator` chains are not available in exec, `Seq` provides the same operations in spec: `s.filter(|x| p(x))`, `s.map_values(|x| f(x))`, `s.subrange(lo, hi)`, `s.update(i, x)`, `s.contains(x)`. **When exec uses a while loop to implement filter/map, the ensures should still use Seq::filter/map_values to express the intent declaratively.**

**Map::dom():** Returns `Set<K>`. Use for "all keys satisfy P": `forall|k| m.dom().contains(k) ==> P(m[k])`. Without this, you can't quantify over Map keys.

## True Limitations (cannot work around in spec)

| Feature | Impact on Spec |
|---------|---------------|
| `async fn` / `await` | Cannot write requires/ensures. Must use `#[verifier::external]`. |
| `f32`/`f64` arithmetic in spec | Cannot reason about float results. |
| `static mut` | No spec model. |
| `transmute` | No spec model. |

'm noticing a discrepancy in the kernel crate's external_
body declarations—everything in the global allowed list from tcb-allowed.md should appear
in phys.rs, but none of them actually do. The spec file has an external_type_specification on
ExFrameNumber, yet it's missing from the detail list, which is puzzling.
Looking
at the per-module scan results, the phys module only reported one
cfg-gated exec code item and zero external_body declarations, which contrad
icts the presence of ExFrameNumber in phys.spec.rs. I need to understand whether ph
ys.spec.rs is considered part of the module scope and how verify.sh actually computes the per-module cheating gate and
cfg-gate detection.

# Count cfg-gated exec code (cheating indicator).
# When MODULE is set, counts only for module files; otherwise whole crate.
count_cfg_gates() {
    local scan_dir="$1"
    python3 -c "
import re, sys
from pathlib import Path

src_dir = Path('$scan_dir')
count = 0
cfg_pat = re.compile(r'#\[cfg(_attr)?\((not\()?verus_keep_ghost')

for rs_file in sorted(src_dir.glob('**/*.rs')):
    lines = rs_file.read_text().splitlines()
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not cfg_pat.search(stripped):
            continue
        if 'derive(' in stripped or 'feature(' in stripped:
            continue
        target = ''
        for j in range(i + 1, min(i + 5, len(lines))):
            t = lines[j].strip()
            if not t or t.startswith('#['):
                continue
            target = t
            break
        if any(target.startswith(k) for k in ['use ', 'use(', 'include!', 'extern ', 'mod ']):
            continue
        if re.match(r'(debug_assert|info|error|warn|trace|debug|log)!\s*\(', target):
            continue
        count += 1

print(count)
" 2>/dev/null
}

# --- Determine module-scoped cheating dir (if MODULE is set) ---
MODULE_CHEATING_DIR=""

    if [[ "$MODULE" == "root" ]]; then
        MODULE_CHEATING_DIR=""  # root has no separate dir; skip module-scoped

name: ast-consistency
description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
   - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
4. **If confirmed, document with full justification.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
   comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
   what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.
